name: Database Administration
tagline: Narrow, deep, well-paid — and rarely a first job.
description: Database administrators keep the data safe, available, and fast: backups and restores, performance tuning, access control, upgrades. It pays well and the skills are portable across industries. The honest caveat is that DBA is a smaller field than it used to be — cloud managed services absorbed a lot of routine administration — and it is almost never an entry-level hire. The realistic route is support or analyst work first, then specializing.
avgTimeline: 18–30 months, typically via support, analyst, or developer work first

salaryRange.note: Junior DBA / database support range. BLS reports a $104,620 median for database administrators and architects (May 2024) — genuinely high, but that's the experienced middle of the field, not the entry point.

remoteFriendly.note: Database work is remote-friendly, with on-call rotations common because a database outage is an all-hands emergency.

realityCheck: Fewer pure DBA jobs exist than a decade ago, because AWS RDS and Azure SQL handle patching, backups, and failover automatically. The growing version of this job is 'data platform engineer' — SQL depth plus cloud plus some automation. Plan for that shape rather than the 1990s DBA shape.
whyItFits: This suits people who like being the person responsible for something that absolutely cannot break. It's methodical, procedure-heavy work where carefulness is the core professional virtue — a good fit if inventory accuracy or cash handling was the part of past jobs you were reliably good at.

motivation.quote: Nobody thanks the DBA for the backup. They thank the DBA for the restore — once, and they never forget it.
motivation.story: A common route: someone in a support or reporting role becomes the person who writes the SQL nobody else can, takes over report maintenance, then inherits database housekeeping when the previous owner leaves. Specialization often arrives by adoption rather than by application — you become the database person by being the one who keeps solving database problems.
motivation.source: Composite of the pattern described in r/SQLServer and r/Database career threads

interviewPrep.question: This query is slow. How do you find out why?
interviewPrep.why: The central DBA question. Look at the execution plan, check for missing or unused indexes, look for table scans, check statistics freshness, check for implicit conversions and non-sargable predicates, consider parameter sniffing.

interviewPrep.question: What's the difference between a clustered and a non-clustered index, and what's the cost of adding one?
interviewPrep.why: Clustered defines physical row order (one per table); non-clustered is a separate structure with pointers. The cost: every index slows down writes and consumes storage.

interviewPrep.question: Explain RPO and RTO, and how your backup strategy delivers them.
interviewPrep.why: RPO is how much data you can afford to lose; RTO is how long you can afford to be down. Full plus differential plus transaction log backups, with the log frequency set by the RPO.

interviewPrep.question: How do you know your backups actually work?
interviewPrep.why: The only correct answer is that you restore them on a schedule to a test server. Anyone who says 'the job reports success' fails this question.

interviewPrep.question: What are ACID properties?
interviewPrep.why: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability. Be ready to give a concrete example of each — a funds transfer is the standard one.

interviewPrep.question: A production database is at 100% CPU during business hours. What are your first steps?
interviewPrep.why: Identify the top consuming queries, check for blocking and long-running transactions, check for a recently changed plan or a missing index, mitigate first (kill the runaway query, add capacity) and root-cause after.

interviewPrep.question: How do you control who can see sensitive data?
interviewPrep.why: Principle of least privilege, roles rather than per-user grants, views or column-level permissions, encryption at rest and in transit, and audit logging.

steps.title: Learn SQL to real depth
steps.description: Deeper than the analyst level: joins and aggregation, then subqueries, CTEs, window functions, transactions and isolation levels, stored procedures, views, and constraints. You should be able to read someone else's 200-line query and explain what it does and why it's slow.
steps.costNote: Free. Every major database engine has a free edition and free official documentation.
steps.outcome: You can write, read, and debug complex SQL, including procedural code.
steps.resumeBullet: Advanced SQL: complex joins, window functions, CTEs, stored procedures, transaction isolation, and query debugging.

resources.name: PostgreSQL Tutorial
resources.notes: Free, thorough, and PostgreSQL itself is free and open source.

resources.name: SQLZoo (free interactive exercises)
resources.notes: Free, browser-based — usable on a library computer or a phone.

resources.name: Microsoft SQL Server documentation and free Developer Edition
resources.notes: Free documentation; SQL Server Developer Edition is free for non-production use and is the full product.

resources.name: Use The Index, Luke! (free SQL indexing book)
resources.notes: Free online. The clearest explanation of indexing and query performance available anywhere.

steps.title: Learn database design and normalization
steps.description: Primary and foreign keys, normal forms through 3NF, when denormalization is the right call, data types and why choosing them badly costs you later, and entity-relationship modeling. Design a schema for something you understand — a store's inventory and sales, a warehouse's pick-and-pack flow — and defend the design choices.
steps.costNote: Free. dbdiagram.io and draw.io both have free tiers for modeling.
steps.outcome: A normalized schema you designed, with the reasoning documented.
steps.resumeBullet: Designed normalized relational schemas with appropriate keys, constraints, indexing strategy, and documented entity-relationship models.

resources.name: dbdiagram.io (free ER modeling)
resources.notes: Free tier. Text-to-diagram, which makes schemas easy to version and share.

resources.name: Database Design course (freeCodeCamp, free)
resources.notes: Free full course covering normalization and modeling.

steps.title: Install and run your own database servers
steps.description: Install PostgreSQL and SQL Server Developer Edition locally or in VMs. Load a large sample database, then practice the actual job: take backups, deliberately destroy the database, and restore it. Do a point-in-time restore. Break it in new ways. This is the single most important hands-on step on this path.
steps.costNote: Free. PostgreSQL is open source; SQL Server Developer Edition and Oracle Database Express Edition are both free for non-production use.
steps.outcome: You have restored a database from backup, including to a point in time, more than once.
steps.resumeBullet: Administered PostgreSQL and SQL Server instances in a lab environment: installation, configuration, backup strategy, point-in-time recovery, and user/permission management.

resources.name: PostgreSQL (free, open source)
resources.notes: Free. The most in-demand open-source database.

resources.name: SQL Server Developer Edition (free)
resources.notes: Free for development and testing — the full Enterprise feature set, licensed for non-production use.

resources.name: Sample databases (AdventureWorks, StackOverflow, Pagila)
resources.notes: Free. Brent Ozar's StackOverflow sample database is large enough to make performance tuning real.

resources.name: Brent Ozar's free SQL Server training and blog
resources.notes: Substantial free content on performance tuning and DBA practice; paid courses optional.

steps.title: Learn performance tuning
steps.description: Reading execution plans, understanding index strategy, spotting blocking and deadlocks, statistics, and the query patterns that defeat indexes. This is where DBAs earn their salaries and it is the hardest skill on this path — expect it to take months rather than weeks.
steps.costNote: Free. The best material on this subject is published free by consultants as marketing.
steps.outcome: You can take a slow query and make it fast, and explain why it was slow.
steps.resumeBullet: Performance-tuned SQL workloads: execution plan analysis, index design, statistics maintenance, and resolution of blocking and deadlock conditions.

resources.name: Use The Index, Luke!
resources.notes: Free online, engine-agnostic, and the best starting point for indexing.

resources.name: Brent Ozar — free 'How to Think Like the SQL Server Engine'
resources.notes: Free training series on execution plans and tuning.

resources.name: PostgreSQL EXPLAIN documentation and explain.depesz.com
resources.notes: Free tool for making PostgreSQL execution plans readable.

steps.title: Learn cloud databases
steps.description: Most new databases are deployed as managed cloud services. Learn AWS RDS or Azure SQL Database: provisioning, automated backups, high availability and failover, read replicas, and how the cloud provider's cost model works. This is what makes the skill set current rather than legacy.
steps.costNote: Nearly free inside cloud free tiers — budget $0–15 for accidental overruns and set a billing alarm before you provision anything.
steps.outcome: You've run a managed cloud database including a failover test.
steps.resumeBullet: Deployed and managed cloud databases (AWS RDS / Azure SQL): provisioning, automated backup and restore, high availability configuration, and cost management.

resources.name: AWS RDS documentation and free tier
resources.notes: Free tier available for 12 months on eligible instance types. Set a billing alarm first.

resources.name: Microsoft Azure Data Fundamentals (DP-900)
resources.notes: PAID, around $99 in the US (regional pricing varies). Cheap, respected, and the free Microsoft Learn path is sufficient preparation.

steps.title: A database certification
steps.description: Certification matters more in this field than in software engineering but less than in networking. Azure Database Administrator (DP-300) and Oracle's associate-level credentials are the recognizable ones. Oracle certs in particular are expensive — pursue those only if local job listings ask for Oracle specifically.
steps.costNote: PAID: Azure DP-300 is $165; Oracle Database Administration associate-level exams run roughly $245 plus often-recommended paid training. Verify local demand before buying, and ask an employer to fund it.
steps.resumeBullet: Microsoft Certified: Azure Database Administrator Associate (DP-300).

resources.name: Azure Database Administrator Associate (DP-300)
resources.notes: PAID, $165. Free official learning path available on Microsoft Learn.

resources.name: Oracle Database certifications
resources.notes: PAID, roughly $245 per exam. Oracle skills pay well but are concentrated in large enterprises — check demand in your area first.

resources.name: Oracle MyLearn (free training)
resources.notes: Free official Oracle training content; the exams are the paid part.

steps.title: Get to databases through an adjacent role
steps.description: Very few organizations hire a junior DBA off the street. They do hire report developers, SQL developers, application support analysts, and data analysts — and those people end up owning database work. Target those titles, then volunteer for the backup checks, the index review, and the slow-query investigations nobody else wants.
steps.outcome: Database responsibility on your actual job description.
steps.resumeBullet: Owned database maintenance responsibilities including backup verification, index maintenance, and query performance investigation.

resources.name: Indeed — SQL developer and database analyst listings
resources.notes: Free. Search 'SQL developer', 'report developer', 'database analyst', and 'application support' — these are the realistic on-ramps.

resources.name: r/SQLServer and r/PostgreSQL
resources.notes: Free. Practitioner communities where the realistic career path gets discussed openly.

resources.name: PASS Data Community / local SQL user groups
resources.notes: Free local user groups and free SQL Saturday events — a reliable place to meet people who hire DBAs.
